utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. It is hoped that Judge Van den Wyngaert will be able to sit after the next break. We will, for the time being, continue two of us sitting under the Rule. Now, Mr. Moore, are you ready? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would just remind the witness that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Thank you

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have one or two questions to ask you. General Vasiljevic, he came to Vukovar, I believe, on the 19th; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What position did General Vasiljevic hold at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic was the chief of the security administration of the Yugoslav People's Army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that he came and he was discussing various matters with individuals who were there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in our premises, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you aware of a document that arrived, I believe from memory, it was the 18th of November, that came to Major Sljivancanin. We have heard about it here that it came from General Vasiljevic indicating that every effort should be made for Croatian soldiers to be detained to facilitate exchange with JNA soldiers. Were you aware of that policy or document?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So not aware of the document. What about the policy of: Let's see if we can get as many Croatian soldiers so that we can exchange them for some of ours who have been detained, just prisoner for prisoner. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall having been aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you wouldn't be aware of Sljivancanin speaking to Vukasinovic about that topic; would be that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I presume that means that you weren't aware. Can you explain to me, then, the following phrase, that when -- I think you were at the barracks on the -- it might have been Negoslavci, on the 19th of November, that you remember a Colonel Tumanov being present?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presence of Colonel Tumanov sticks in my memory because of this thing he did when he withdrew his hands because this was a rather ridiculous situation. He extended his hand to treat Marin Vidic Bili and then he withdrew his hand. And that's why I remember the scene, the arrival of Colonel Tumanov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you do remember him being there, it's as simple as that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you explain to me how Major Sljivancanin was having a heated conversation with the very head of his department? The phrase you were -- that you told us yesterday was that you heard "a fairly heated conversation between Sljivancanin and Vasiljevic." I'm just curious how it is a major can have a heated conversation with his boss. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the conversation took place in the hallway outside of our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our office in Negoslavci, yes. So it was in the hallway right out of the office. It was a loud conversation. And the topic of the conversation is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But what I'm curious about - I didn't know about the location so we'll deal with that - "fairly heated," that, I would suggest, tends to indicate that there were raised voices, voices that were angry. Would that be a fair way of assessing it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way. It was an angry conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: An angry conversation between a general and a major; that's correct, isn't it, in a public place?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the office or rather in the hallway outside of the office, my impression was that they were angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, but sometimes when one has disagreements, one tries to have those disagreements in offices. This angry exchange was in a hallway between a general and a major. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't go into guessing why it was in the hallway, it was in the hallway and that's more or less the only thing I know. I don't know anything apart from what I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It wouldn't have been, perhaps, Major Sljivancanin indicating that he was not happy with General Vasiljevic's position of trying to take J -- Croatian prisoners in exchange for JNA prisoners, was it, and expressing his dissatisfaction with that policy? Are you able to help us?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't because I don't know what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When was it that Vasiljevic gave you the task of collecting the items and taking those items to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given the task by Mr. Sljivancanin and I remember that he had told me that it was General Vasiljevic who had ordered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move to the 20th. I've already dealt with this topic in very general terms but I'll deal with it now more particularly. At what time did you get to the barracks, approximately, on the morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime between 10.00 and 9.00 I went to the hospital, I stayed there a couple of minutes, and went back to the barracks. That's the period that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you went to the hospital -- you say you were there a couple of minutes -- so if people say that they saw you, you would agree that you were at the hospital, but you say just a couple of minutes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for just a couple of minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you go into the hospital grounds?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if you weren't in the hospital grounds, presumably you weren't in the hospital, were you?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the grounds, I was there at the entrance, at the gate. I was not in the building itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, who did you speak to at the gate?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. When we asked where the forensic technicians were, some commanding officers present there said that they had headed towards the barracks. I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, when you went to the hospital, did you see the buses lined up outside?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing Mr. Sljivancanin at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw him, but he is far away from me. I think I saw him. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Karan?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I suppose it's pointless to ask whether you saw Mr. Radic. Did you see Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's not a case of them not being there, it's a case of you not seeing these people because you were there for such a short time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there for just a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you went to the hospital, where did you travel from, Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In what vehicle did you travel?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a police Puch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How was it that you were able to get to the hospital at a time when other people were not able to get there, by the way over the bridge?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like Mr. Moore to confront the witness, to tell him who claimed that it was impossible to get to the hospital at that time and what route we're talking about. I think that would be fair to the witness in light of what the witness has testified about his arrival at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't see a basis at the moment, for interfering, Mr. Bulatovic. We'll watch it. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no problems getting there. There were no problems there at the hospital, if that's what you mean. If you mean that the road had been destroyed. I really don't know what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you know Vukovar or you knew Vukovar in 1991. It's right to say that you know and did know at that time that there were two principal bridges across the River Vuka; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were bridges there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And we have heard evidence from a number of people, monitors, et cetera, where they say that they were in a long queue and we have seen video evidence of it that they could not get across the bridge until 10.00 or thereabouts. What I want to know is how you managed to get across to the hospital at a time when they were told it wasn't possible. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as I already said, I don't know the time, the actual hour, I just said that we got there with Momcilovic and then that we didn't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, but you do know the time and I asked you about that and you went 10.00, 9.00, and you were there approximately two minutes and we have got evidence that suggests that that bridge wasn't open until after that. So I would like to know how you got there.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, 9.00, 10.00, I don't see why that should be a problem to have it plus or minus half an hour, it could be half an hour more than I said. We didn't have any problems getting there. There was some gunfire, we could hear it, but we had no problems as we travelled there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking about gunfire, I'm talking about a long line of traffic with ECMM vehicles, Red Cross vehicles, other vehicles that couldn't get across one of the bridges and I want to know how you were able to get across into the hospital. Do you understand? So can you give us an answer on that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was it the case that there was a checkpoint on the bridge to stop any traffic?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In any event, when you go back, you say that you go to the barracks and you then notice incidents occurring at the barracks themselves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw an unusual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, just describe the unusual situation. A number of people in and around the buses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were buses there in the barracks. The police were there around them and then some 10 to 15 metres away from the buses, there was a group of people, maybe 40 to 50 people, most of them men. The situation was unusual in that there were curses, verbal abuse hurled and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it was much worse than that, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it was a situation that caused you concern, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not concern. This was not a situation that would cause concern but some degree of unease, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I just read to you -- MR. MOORE: I think perhaps in fairness to everybody, that I should just pass out some of the transcripts that we have, with the Court's leave, I'd ask to do that. It's marked up in a way that I would hope would help for B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could that be done now, please. The Defence can have them if they wish; I have no problems with that. Will that help? Of course. It's exactly the same format as we have used on previous occasions. There is a chronological index. Items one and two are the 12th of November, 1998. Three and four, 1st of October, 2001. Three is English and one is English. Then number five is an English and B/C/S translation by an OTP investigator Nigel Stewart. Six and seven, the 5th of November, 2003. Six is English, seven, B/C/S. Eight and nine, transcripts from the main hearing, 23rd of November at Belgrade. Ten and eleven, an audio recording, 11th of November. English is ten. And then finally, you may remember, perhaps not, number twelve where you and I had a chat in Belgrade on the 19th of September. I hope you remember that. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's us then deal, if we may, with tab 8, please, and for you, it is B/C/S, which is 9. So in English it is tab 8, page 7, bottom right-hand corner; for the B/C/S equivalent, it is page 0367-9153. Mr. Karanfilov, we tend to have our numbers on the top right-hand corner in the B/C/S, so yours should be 0367-9153. Have you got that page?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm just going to read, it's on the top of the page, I think, the B/C/S. "Inside the barracks compound," and this is you speaking with the judge asking the question. "Inside the barracks compound, and what we found, so to say, the most striking and unacceptable at the same time, was that there was a lot of civilians surrounding the buses who were expressing rather fierce anger." Have you got that passage?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean by "rather fierce anger"? That's not the way you have described it here at all, is it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, fierce anger, that's what I meant, actually very bad curses hurled at those people involving members of their family and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's move on in that page, it's the English page, page 8, it's half of the way down the page. The Presiding Judge asks the question: "When you were questioned by the investigating judge of the military court, did you actually say, 'as far as I could gather, their intention was to take over the securing of the buses'? "Karanfilov: Yes. "Question: Is that what you were saying? "Yes, it was literally like that. They almost scuffled with the police," that's military police, "but this did not happen, although that's how it looked like. I'm not saying that that I am right, this is my personal opinion."

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we'll wait for the question, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem with interpretation or translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we'll have the question and answer and then you can put that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So have you got that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Go to page 0367-9153. Top right-hand corner. Have you got that page number?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It should be 9153, I would say it is halfway down the page. It's a question -- I can lead it in a little earlier. Let's see if we can find that. Deputy prosecutor: "In what way did they express their desire to take over these people from the buses, what specifically, apart from what he's already told us? Were there any other manifestations like that?" Witness Borco Karanfilov: Well, I believe aside for the insults but I don't know what you mean precisely." Have you got that now?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "Nothing but insults, only insults and swearing; is that right? "Yes, yes, yes." When you were questioned by the investigating judge of the military court, did you actually say: "As far as I could gather, their intention was to take over the securing of the buses?" "Yes. "Is that what you are saying. "Yes, it was literally like that. They almost scuffled with the police but this did not happen, although that's how it looked like. I am not saying that I am right. This is my personal opinion." Now, you see that. Does that now refresh your memory on what you saw on the morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say it once again. This is what it actually says here. It was all at the verbal level and my observation was that this was on the verbal level and this creates an unpleasant picture. When you see a group of people verbally insulting other people, hurling abuse, insults, that's not a pleasant picture, but that's all there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is a difference, I'd suggest; for example, if I am verbally insulted, well, one can live with that. But this is a situation where you have a group of people who are in a bus or buses who allegedly have been responsible for criminal acts. And the people who are outside are suggesting that many of these criminal acts were committed against them or their family. That is right, isn't it? Such things as murder; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true or at least I assume that there were people on the buses who may or may not have committed criminal offences. The locals probably had reason enough to abuse them and curse them. Many of them had lost their nearest and dearest so probably that was reason enough for them to abuse those people and jeer at them. If that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's not quite what I mean at all. There may be a reason for jeering and abusing, but one also has to put into the context what those people believe they have suffered and what they are also capable of inflicting. And those people, I'd suggest, some of them had weapons. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were armed people there, but that is very much a hypothetical question. What would have been the case if something else had gone on to happen differently. I have already given you all my observations and all my conclusions regarding this situation. I can't address what might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, in actual fact, you can address what might have been because what might have been actually did become. Those people were murdered. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I don't know about that. I entered the barracks on a mission. I was there for several minutes. My impression and observation is a near snapshot and that's what I'm telling you. My impression was that the situation was under control and that the commander was keeping the entire situation under control and there was no reason to believe anything else, nothing to lead me to believe otherwise, nor was I required to do anything about that or linger there. So this is a snapshot impression that I garnered in the brief time that I spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Firstly, I would suggest to you that what you say is an attempt to minimise what was going on because you, in actual fact, were so concerned, you mentioned it to Lukic who was in charge of security at the barracks; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic was standing at a distance of about 25 or 30 metres. He was aware of what was going on. I talked to him much along the lines of asking him what was going down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you did speak to Lukic.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you used the phrase "we informed Lukic," in that interview that I've referred to. Who's "we"?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. We informed him, that's probably about the brief conversation that we had. When I say "we," I mean Zoran Momcilovic and I, since we happened to be there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you don't need to, to inform him of anything, do you, if he's just standing there and can see; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree. That's precisely why I think the word "to inform" has two potential meanings in this context. There was an exchange saying things like: "What is going on? What was this about?" It's not like I was informing the commander. The commander was there, he was monitoring the situation and he was commanding his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I would suggest it's of more than that, that you informed Sljivancanin about the problems; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't see that as a problem. I did inform Sljivancanin. I had the impression that he had already found out earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where did you get the impression that he had found out earlier on?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was based on him saying that everything was all right. I think his answer was "Everything is all right."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, "everything is all right" can mean many things. I'm asking you why do you say you formed the impression that he already knew?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely because he asked no additional questions. I assume that had he had any other questions or had he not known about the situation, he would have asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You earlier on, about three or four minutes ago said that it was not your duty to do anything, along those lines; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that what I actually did was doing anything about it, informing someone or, rather, talking to Mr. Sljivancanin, is not for me tantamount to me doing anything particular about the situation at the barracks. What I was required to do was to observe and to convey my observations to the chief, so this is a mere observation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Please go again to, in your case, tab 9, English tab 8, page 7. The B/C/S equivalent 0367-9153. It's the same page that I was referring to earlier. So English it's tab 8, page 7, bottom of the page. And for the B/C/S, it is at the top of page 0367-9153. I've already mentioned this to you but I want to read now extra parts. At the top of the page of the B/C/S, "And what we found, so to say, the most striking and unacceptable at the same time, was that there was a lot of civilians surrounding the buses who were expressing rather fierce anger. Later, since the police were around the buses, after that, which means while we were taking over Bili we informed Lukic who had just been appointed commander of the barracks, and I think that upon our return to Negoslavci, we informed Sljivancanin as well that local residents were gathering around some buses in the barracks. I guess that this is what the gentleman was referring to." So there you have that you in -- you see an incident, you mention it to Lukic, and then you mention it to Sljivancanin back in Negoslavci. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I -- there seems to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, Mr. Bulatovic is waiting. You're next. I see that Mr. Bulatovic's problem is resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moore read out the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Waiting for the subject matter to reach the end and then we'll come to the concerns. So if you'd wait, Mr. Vasic. We wait on you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought Mr. Vasic wanted something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, he's waiting for you. At my invitation, I might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I politely inquire what he's waiting for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Here you are, Mr. Vasic, jump in quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm waiting for the interpretation. My learned friend, when he quoted the portion from that page -- I'm not sure if the witness had informed Sljivancanin upon returning to Negoslavci with Bili. I think that's one thing that didn't make it into the transcript, page 15, lines 23 through 25, as well as page 16, line 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I just read the part that I have on the B/C/S translation. The witness agrees with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I also deal with tab 3, please. It's tab 4 for you, Mr. Karanfilov. For the English, this is a record compiled on the 1st of October before the military court. And the part I want to deal with is English page 5. For the B/C/S, it is tab 4, page number 0218-8552. Now that should, in the B/C/S, start: "The only thing I remember if that's dates tally was that at the time, I received an order to take charge of an guard Marin Vidic, always known as Bili. Then there's Vesna Bosanac too. We guarded her in the hospital in Negoslavci, completely secretly because we feared reprisals." Have you got that part? Then we go to page 5 in the English. Have you found that part, Mr. Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's the next part that I wanted to deal with. "I think when I took charge of Marin Vidic from the barracks that day, I noticed a large crowd at the barracks around some parked buses because I then saw a group of territorials arguing with our army members around the buses that had people inside. From what I could make out, they wanted to take charge of security of the buses. I cannot now state definitely what this altercation was over. When I returned to the command in Negoslavci, I think I informed Sljivancanin about it but I do not know what action he then took." So you have, on previous occasions, informed courts in 2001 and later on, I think it's 2004, that you told Sljivancanin when you returned to Negoslavci. That's right, isn't it, that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of course, your account here is different, isn't it? Your account here is that you spoke to Sljivancanin when he was in Vukovar. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I mentioned this to Mr. Sljivancanin upon leaving the shelter when we were off with those documents that we had taken. We met him somewhere near the exhibit in the vicinity of the shelter. Why am I saying that? I'm saying that because as we were coming out and we met, Sljivancanin asked if we had observed a vehicle, a car with foreign licence plates near the shelter. We had, in fact, observed one and the idea was to go back and take the licence plates off because they were foreign licence plates. That's why I remember Sljivancanin as being there, because we had to go back and get the foreign licence plates off that vehicle there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is: Now I'm saying that I saw Sljivancanin in Vukovar. Is that the answer to my question, not Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Because we have heard evidence that Mr. Sljivancanin didn't get back to Negoslavci until around about 6.00ish in the evening. He was going back to the command briefing and that he was seen by Major Vukasinovic that evening and then saw him afterwards in Negoslavci. So if that's the case, and these accounts that you gave earlier on are true, it means quite simply that you weren't making a trip to Belgrade from Vukovar, you were seeing Sljivancanin in Negoslavci; isn't that right, later in the evening.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand at all the permutation of events. I'm telling you, it's been a long time, it's been 15 years. Even now, I could hardly claim that I saw that car, had I not seen that recording with that armoured car. And this car sticks with me because of its foreign licence plates. I'm not sure with a other information you may or may not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Am I right that in actual fact on the account that you have given to courts previously, you would be seeing Sljivancanin not in Vukovar, but in Negoslavci in the area of the command post. That's what you believed when you gave this evidence; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that would mean that you were wrong about travelling back to Belgrade on the 20th because, quite simply, you would be travelling at night and wouldn't get back for some considerable time; that is also right, isn't it? Isn't it, Mr. Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That changes nothing at all about the fact I could have gone on to Belgrade. I don't see why not. Actually, I have no idea what you're trying to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think you know perfectly well what I'm trying to suggest and indeed I am suggesting that if this account that you gave to the judges is correct, that you were in and around the command post when Sljivancanin was there, and you were therefore not in Belgrade, and that in actual fact you were the officer who went to Ovcara and released the military police; isn't that right, Mr. Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Come on, sir. Please. First of all, this piece of information that suggests that I went to Ovcara and conveyed this, that is just not true. Out of the question. I'm not an officer. I am no part of the chain of command. I was not an officer in the chain of command in a position to impart orders to anyone. The gentleman you're talking about is a military police officer. He takes his orders down the chain of command. One of his commanders, his superiors, had given him a task, to set up a group, to take up a position and securing the hangar. These are military tasks and they are very specific. In a chain of command, an order can be withdrawn by an officer of the same rank or his superior. Members of any counter-intelligence group have no authority to impart any orders or withdraw any orders. Therefore, your theory is erroneous, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's not my theory. There are three witnesses who say you were at Ovcara on the 20th. There are the following: There is Vezmarovic who said that you were there. There is 022 who says that you were there. And 001 says that you were there. So you have three separate independent people who say that you were at Ovcara on the 20th. Let's deal with the generalities and come to the specifics. It's right, on your account that you have given this court, that you were never at Ovcara on the 20th; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was never at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So dealing with the generalities, you were not at Ovcara on the 20th. That is correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So these three people, all independent people, all giving evidence here, said they saw you there. Do you understand that? Have you been told that by Mr. Lukic, or in your case, Mr. Bulatovic? Have you been told that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I was told about the security commander. Please, again, I'm telling you, the last name that I referred to in relation to the fact that I introduced myself on the day of the Mitnica Battalion surrender, I still believe that to have been an honourable thing to do. There is that last name that was dropped in relation to the security commander. I'm telling you, this is an insinuation and a fabrication and the whole story was staged, as it were, at a later stage just because people knew my name. This whole story is a fabrication and there is not the blindest bit of truth to it. The security commander must take his orders from somebody in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's set aside the chain of command. Don't bother looking at Mr. Lukic, Mr. Bulatovic, they're not going to help you.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. My apologies, again, but again, you're way off the mark. Somebody was springing to their feet, and that's the actual reason I turned around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There are three people who saw you there. One of them saw you on the 18th in daylight. He saw you again for over an hour on the 19th - this is on your evidence - and he gave evidence that you recognised you and knew who you were the following day when you told him to withdraw the military police and indeed introduced him to a TO leader who was going to take over. So you're saying, therefore, the identification is wrong; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying the whole thing is a lie. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you keep saying your name is well-known. Mr. Sljivancanin, we have heard he was being picked out because his name was well-known. How is your name known? You were only a minor officer. You've told us that already.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I didn't say my family name was a well-known one. I said it was a rather peculiar sounding one because it doesn't end in the usual "ic," which is common in B/C/S. I said my last name was peculiar and therefore easy to remember, because it somewhat deviates from the norm in the B/C/S. Those are the very words I used. Don't twist it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I want to know why on earth you, Borco Karanfilov, should have the finger pointed by three separate people as being responsible for the pulling out of the military police, thereby guaranteeing the slaughter of over 200 people. What is it that you have done to people to deserve this?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think the simple reason is my family name was the only one they knew because it is a peculiar sounding one. But I can't rule out the possibility that they're trying to shift the blame to someone else because of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's look at it again. You were not at Ovcara -- on the 20th, therefore you were not with Vukasinovic on the 20th, clearly, at Ovcara; that is right, it's just logical.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Belgrade on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you were not with Vukasinovic on the 18th either, were you, at Ovcara, because we have heard your evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in actual fact, these witnesses refer to you being with Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't know who said what. One thing I am certain about is it's a blatant lie. The more I like at it, the more I see people are trying to shift the blame to someone else in order to exonerate themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the one thing that is absolutely certain is you were not with Vukasinovic on the 18th, that is right, when you were at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic: Velepromet. You and I had a chat with Velepromet and I seem to remember you had some difficulty remembering that location. Do you remember that conversation?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And just to assist the Court, my learned friends have got the B/C/S equivalent but it's at divider 12. It is page 5 of 13, so English page 5 of 13, divider 12 of the English translation. Now, I asked you one-fifth of the way down the page the following question -- I'm MM and you're BK, surprisingly: "Who was that? Who was that someone? "Okay. "Let's deal with Velepromet. Do you know the Velepromet facility?" The answer that you gave: "It's a bit foggy." I then asked the question: "You don't remember Velepromet, the main area for the evacuation." "I remember it was opposite the barracks or something like that," was the answer. Then you go on to say quite simply about the road dividing them. Now what I want to ask you is this, you were security organ and Borisavljevic was a security organ and we have seen documentation here indicate that go Borisavljevic had, and I will use a neutral word, responsibility for the Velepromet collection facility. You were aware of that fact, obviously. Yes?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of the fact that in the early days in Negoslavci, Borisavljevic went to the barracks and he spent all of his time there. I wasn't aware of his specific responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I suggest that cannot be right because there were security organ briefings by Sljivancanin to which Borisavljevic attended; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all. Again, where meetings were held very much depended on how much time people had and the overall situation. Briefings and informing the chief about the situation, well that's a different matter. The security organ discussed only what was material to their work. We didn't necessarily familiarise ourselves with what everybody else throughout the security organ was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. We'll cut it down to fine bones. You knew that Borisavljevic was at Velepromet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know that he was in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking about the barracks, as you're well aware. I'm talking about Velepromet. Or do you see them as being a similar ...

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see as being similar. You are asking me if I was aware of that. The only thing I was aware of was his office at the barracks. I didn't know about Velepromet and him there. He was billeted at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you were asked about Velepromet in other court sessions don't you remember that occurring? I think it was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you to go to 5E, please, of the divider and I hope it is page 14. So 5E. And it is line at 19, 20. This is the 2003 interview. You are asked a question about Velepromet and at 19, you say "I have a vague picture of Velepromet." In your case, it would be line 16, line 24. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 5E.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It should be orange. So go to line 19 and 20, page 14 of 17. It is concurrently a translation. Have you now got that, Mr. Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The translation that we have got is "I have a vague picture of Velepromet ..." Have you got? "But at that time, nobody really dared to walk around Velepromet. "Why was that, fear?" Line 28: "It was war." Well, now, Velepromet was within the zone of responsibility for OG South; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said last time that I don't know about Operations Group. I did not know about south, east, and so on but as for Velepromet, it was near the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can we just work on a slight inference that if it's near the barracks and near Vukovar, that it might be under the control of Mr. Mrksic and his troops. Can we work on that basis?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you just explain to me then please the phrase "But at that time, nobody really dared to walk around Velepromet." Could you explain to me why people couldn't walk around Velepromet, why you've given that answer, and it was war?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, the answer I gave was: "I don't know," full stop. "I don't know," full stop. "Let me tell you, I have this foggy picture, approximately, of that part of Velepromet, but at that time, nobody dared to walk around or to walk and walk around." This is not -- I'm not talking about walking around Velepromet; no, walking around in general. The first question was related to Velepromet, and my answer was that I have a vague picture of Velepromet. And the second part of my answer pertains to the whole area. After dark, nobody dared to walk around at all, not just around Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So this answer refers to the area generally, not the Velepromet facility that was where the TO were based as we have heard; is that right? Or the suggestion of lawlessness?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let me try and put it to you. I would suggest people didn't walk around Velepromet because the Velepromet facility was used for filtering individuals who were brought in, that the TO were actively involved there, and that it was an extremely dangerous place for people to go. That's all I'm suggesting.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, please, I don't agree with your allegation. "I don't know. I don't know. Let me tell you, I have this foggy picture." This is the sentence that I actually stated recently now. "I have this foggy vague picture of Velepromet,"; the second part of the sentence is, "and -- but at that time, nobody dared to walk, to walk around." This pertains to the whole war zone in general when, after nightfall, nobody walked around unless one really need today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's put it to the test. Would you read out the exact words, please, of line 16 in B/C/S, and the interpreters can interpret. Would you do that? Starting, "Neznam. Neznam."

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I don't know. I don't know. At that time let me tell you, I have this foggy picture approximately of this part of Velepromet, but at that time, nobody dared to walk or to walk around."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you say, then, it relates to the area generally, not just the Velepromet facility?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to deal with two other topics before I finish. When were you at the military academy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you meet any of these defendants when you were there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I can't speak for the Defence counsel, but I was only going to ask about the defendants. I won't ask about the Defence counsel. Just the three defendants: Mr. Mrksic, we'll leave out Mr. Bulatovic, Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was interpreter's error.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, Mr. Radic or Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long was Mr. Radic at the academy with you for?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you would consider yourself a friend of Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I think it's also right to say that you have told a previous court that he would come a number of times to the post at Negoslavci; is that right? Mr. Radic, that is.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said many times. I think I said several times. He did come there a couple of times, a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can I just put the following sentence to you. It's at line 5020 -- actually, page 5020, line 3. It was in respect of the following question: "Do you know Captain -- did you know captain Karanfilov before the 20th of November? "Yes. He came with Major Sljivancanin to the headquarters of my company in Nova Ulica," and he then went on to describe you. Is that right? Did you go to Nova Ulica with Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not enter Vukovar at all during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if in actual fact your friend, Captain Radic, was there, are you saying you didn't keep contact with him or to go to see if he was there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go there because that was not my task. I didn't visit any of the units except for the rear units in Berak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I would suggest you did go and see him there. Can I finish, then, in the following way. You told us that you got documents and you went off to Belgrade with those documents; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Those documents themselves were burnt documents; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them. It was obvious that somebody had tried to set fire to them on purpose. Some papers had burned down and some were still intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I would like to know is this: You had a perfectly good warrant officer; isn't that right at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what you mean "a good warrant officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you know perfectly well what I mean. That in actual fact, you had another person in the security organ who was a lesser rank to yourself. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not have a warrant officer in the security organ. He was a member, just as myself, and apart from the chief and the two deputies, all the other members of the security organ are at the same level, regardless of the actual rank they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. I'm using British ranking system. What I want to know quite simply is this: Why is it necessary for two members of the security organ to have to go all the way to Belgrade when in actual fact it is an extremely busy time for the security organ to be there? Why waste two people rather than just one?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going to question Major Sljivancanin's order. I am not competent to judge why he did issue that order. It is a fact that we did not know what we would find there and how much material there would be. And you will agree with me that it would be difficult for one person -- it would be risky for one person to go there, to collect all that material and then to go with all that material to Belgrade because it was war. The war was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You see, what I would suggest to you is that in actual fact, when you have been spoken to at earlier dates about when you went to Belgrade, what you actually said was as follows: "I cannot say for sure exactly when I left Vukovar because I cannot -- or I really cannot remember." Do you remember saying that? Just -- actually in fairness: "But I am certain that I returned three to five days before the unit did." So there you are saying: I cannot say for sure exactly when I left Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep saying in all my statements I am talking about the events. I remember events, I don't remember the dates, and that is why I said even in that statement that I cannot be sure about the actual dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I'm going to ask you to look at this. It's the English tab 3, B/C/S tab 4. English tab 3, it is page 8, paragraph 11. The B/C/S, 0218-8553. So I want to go to -- it would be approximately three-fifths of the way down the B/C/S page. Paragraph 11. "I do not remember any kind of written order being sent to us from the command regarding the treatment of prisoners in the final phase of the operation, and nor do I remember whether any kind of verbal order was issued in that regard. I cannot say for sure exactly when I left Vukovar because I really cannot remember, but I am certain that I returned three to five days before the unit did." I am suggesting to you, you indicated earlier on you are not sure when it was you went back to Belgrade, if you did. You are saying three to five, so it could be three, could be four, could be five days, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and so what? As far as I'm concerned, it's okay. As I said so many times before, I don't know about the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The "so what" quite simply is this: That you were the officer told to go along and release those military police. And I would suggest that in actual fact, that you, when you did that, knew perfectly well what you were doing and what the consequences would be, namely the murder of these people in Ovcara. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I'm saying that this allegation is completely wrong on your part. Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic -- I think we'd better -- there are ten minutes, Mr. Bulatovic. Would you like a break or would you like to press on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take our break now and then I can continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After the cross-examination by the Prosecution, I will ask you a couple of questions in an effort to clarify a few things that are of great importance to us. Mr. Karanfilov, you remember that you talked to my learned colleague from the Prosecution about the fact that that day in the barracks, you had seen the buses and how long you had stayed there and that after this event, you had gone back to the shelter and you said that you had notified Mr. Sljivancanin. You were told that in some of your statements you had said that this had been in negotiations; now you said that it was at the shelter. Let us clarify now this: Where did you meet Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Sljivancanin near the shelter. I don't know the exact location, but it was close. The reason why I say it was close, because there was a possibility and there was, in fact the need for us to go back to pick up the foreign licence plates on the car that was there at the shelter. In the conversation with Mr. Sljivancanin, as far as I can remember, it was stressed that this foreign vehicle was there and according to some estimates, this vehicle cost about 3 to 400.000 German marks and this is why it was very important for us to be in possession of those licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, I just wanted to know where the conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was near the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And then you went on to Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: From that time on, did you see Mr. Sljivancanin again at all?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not until his return to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about your conversation with Marin Vidic and the fact that General Tumanov appeared there. What I want to know is where this conversation with Marin Vidic took place.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This interview with Mr. Bili was conducted in our office, in the office where we were, in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point conduct any interview with Marin Vidic in the Vukovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the questions by the Prosecutor that had to do with Velepromet, you explained what you had said. Can you please give us the reason why people avoided walking around Vukovar at night? What were the reasons?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not just in Vukovar, in all war zones, when night falls, for safety reasons, this is why you don't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there was curfew in force?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor told you what Captain Vezmarovic had said regarding your encounter, so you were told what Mr. Vezmarovic had said in 2001 and every time you made a statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Since 1991, after seeing Vezmarovic twice in that time, have you ever seen Captain Dragan Vezmarovic again?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never seen him again. That was the only encounter, in fact, the couple of minutes on those two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And did you ever have the occasion to see him during those trials to perhaps talk to him face-to-face to discuss some things?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we go into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You were given those tasks that are related to the hospital, the departure towards the shelter and then on to Belgrade. Was warrant officer Momcilovic with you at all times during that day?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you, and I just realised the OTP asked you the same thing while showing you something. In the briefest possible terms, can you reproduce for us the exact sequence of events of your own activity from the time the Mitnica Battalion surrendered to the time you left for Belgrade? In the briefest possible terms, please.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Preparing the security for Mr. Pavkovic, our departure for the area where the Mitnica Battalion were surrendering, first the preparations then the negotiations then the actual surrender, followed by suggestions --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Slow down, please. I just want to know about the specific steps that you took.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conveying the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to the objection in this form because it's merely a rehearsal in evidence in chief. If there's a specific topic that had been cross-examined on, my learned friend can certainly do that but a rehearsal is certainly inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Technically, Mr. Bulatovic, that is a valid objection. You really, on your question, just asked a witness to summarise what he's already told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll accept that, although I do think that Mr. Moore asked a lot of questions about the 20th and tried to mention something, but okay. I'll try to tackle this in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, your departure for Belgrade, what do you associate that with, any particular events?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to the hospital, I was going back to the barracks, the buses, the shelter, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When answering the questions of Mr. Moore, and once you'd been shown the evidence of witnesses who claimed to have seen you on the 20th, you said these people were whitewashing or shifting their own blame to someone else. Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people who claimed to have seen me there, those specified by the OTP, whoever claimed to have seen me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Why do you think Vezmarovic would possibly have a reason for doing that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Vezmarovic had to have been ordered by his own superior --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object. That just calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's very close to one of your questions, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I asked the question on the basis that people had nominated or indicated that he was there and I asked whether, in actual fact, he could think any reason why it is that they should be saying that. The witness, for example, therefore must have an opportunity of saying, let's us say, I had a fight with Vezmarovic over money and he owes me money and it's a way of getting back. A witness must have an opportunity of being able to clarify that point. In re-examination, I would submit that that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I don't think a distinction can be drawn. Mr. Bulatovic, the concern, though, is the question was put, as I've indicated, very directly by Mr. Moore and the witness has answered it. Are you just going over the same ground again?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not my intention to waste any time, but my learned friend Mr. Moore asked about the reason and the witness said those people were shifting the blame. I just wanted that clarified, what exactly he meant by that, which might be pure speculation on my part, so I'd be happy to give this particular question up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One thing, whether they may be trying to shift the blame. A different issue is why they might do that and that's where you're getting into speculation with the "why." Unless the witness knows something and he has already told us he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, let's move on to something else. You saw an officer on the afternoon of the 18th and on the morning of the 19th. Do you know which unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know which unit was in the area where that building was where they were put up?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at my level. I just knew that he was not one of my own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A military police company, what would be its numerical strength, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would that be sufficient men to set up a security system for this many people?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about reservists? Or assume those people were reservists, would that change things?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no reservists in time of war. Those people are reservists in peacetime. The unit commander who was a police officer is a reserve officer in peacetime conditions but as soon as he's mobilised, he becomes an officer, not a reserve officer. A reserve officer is a peacetime term.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the same term apply to soldiers themselves?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all soldiers are members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to your assignment about the shelter, did you have any other assignments or tasks on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that there were a number of people in the security organ. You told us about their chain of command. What I want to know is, in the JNA, was this chain of command complied with or respected?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that Radic came several times to where you were; right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not our office, our building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me why?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. All I can remember is the phone. I assume that was the reason. That was the only line to Belgrade so maybe officers came to our building to use the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about your relations with Radic. What about your relations with Veselin Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my chief for several months, not more. That's before the actual combat operations and after as well. I was transferred after that and our relations were of a purely professional nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other kind of relations with Mr. Sljivancanin aside from your professional relations?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, you will be pleased to know that that ends the questions that are to be asked of you so you are now free to leave. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance and for the assistance you've given us and the court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just mention one matter to assist my learned friends. With regard to Witness 002, we did, Your Honour, suggest to see whether we could bring that witness in early next Monday and I believe that may well be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Moore. That will be helpful. Could I also mention that it has proved convenient to the listings for our proceedings this Friday to be moved to the morning, 9.00 to 1.45 instead of the afternoon. I had received indications that that would be convenient to a number of people so we have been able to secure that position. So Friday morning will be 9.00 to 1.45 instead of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear Mr. Lukic on account of the atrocious amount of background noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my colleagues. My predictions for this testimony were that it would take longer. Mr. Moore was talking about five hours for Mr. Karanfilov in cross-examination. I was hardly able to secure Mr. Karan's arrival. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, would you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Mladen Karan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: The 16th of September, 1956, in Vojnic, Vojnic municipality, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, please bear in mind what I told you about during your proofing, we have to pause after our questions and answers to ensure an accurate record. I will now go through your CV. Please confirm all of my information for me, if you can. You completed the military gymnasium or high school in 1975 in Belgrade, as far as I know; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was in Belgrade that you attended the military academy for the land forces, which you completed in 1979; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your first professional commitment began that same year. You worked as a commander in a signals platoon for the army's command post in the Bijeljina garrison; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1986, you were off to work with the security bodies. You had been a company commander with that signals unit previously but between 1986 and 1988, you were chief of security of the security branch of the signals regiment in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ever since you worked with the security bodies, between 1988 and 1989, you were the deputy chief of the counter-intelligence group of the 17th JNA Corps based in Tuzla, Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1989, you start working with the security administration in Belgrade and you work in the 1st Intelligence Department of the security administration until the autumn of 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the period we'll be looking at. In the autumn of 1991, you were captain first class; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. From October 1991 to the summer of the following year, roughly speaking, you were assistant chief of security for counter-intelligence in the Guards Motorised Brigade, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your next post is in the cabinet of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence where you worked as a security desk officer within the security department of the cabinet. You remained in that post until the 15th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Between 1993 and 1995, you were chief of security in the 21st Kordun Corps of the Serbian Krajina army; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the Kordun corps, the translation on page 44, line 6, K-o-r-d-u-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the republic of the Serbian Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following operation storm in the summer of 1995, you were back in Belgrade for a couple of days. After this, you take up the post of chief of security of the 11th Slavonia and Baranja Corps of the Serbian Krajina Army in the town of Vukovar; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were there for about 20 days and then you were expelled, as you told the OTP in your interview. You go back to Belgrade. Between 1995 and 2005, you occupied several different posts, but always with the security department of the Ministry of Defence and the JNA, that is the army of Serbia and Montenegro, which was the successor state at one point; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Finally, on the 1st of May, 2005, you retired with the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can now move on to your actual evidence. There's just another thing that strikes me as noteworthy and will probably make for the ease of handling for everybody in these proceedings. You never provided any sort of statement, any sort of official statement to anyone so far. And when I say "official," I mean any official bodies in relation to Vukovar, of course?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: If you disregard yesterday, yes, that holds true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. Yesterday was your first interview to the OTP in their office; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No paperwork for us. Mr. Karan, which precise duties did you have in the security administration in the autumn of 1991? Can you describe that for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I can. I worked in the first operative department of the security administration. My job was the monitoring of any activities by what we called at the time the hostile emigration, which primarily concerned the Albanians living abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Slow down slightly and speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I was also charged with monitoring the activity of the legion etrangere, or rather the members of that organisation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction, the foreign legion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the Yugoslav crisis evolved, I was tasked with monitoring what was going on in Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia, as well as Montenegro and Macedonia. All the former republics with the exception of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This first section or department within the security administration, why is it important? What particular importance does it have?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: That is the main section or the main department. It's called operative. That means it deals with counter-intelligence work throughout the former SFRY, specifically in JNA units and Territorial Defence staffs. I mean their security organs, of course. It provides technical guidance and is superior to everyone in this technical sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to your age and the rank you held at the time, what was your position within that unit in relation to everyone else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I was captain first class at the time and most of the other people were lieutenant-colonels or colonels. However, as a result of the circumstances that prevailed, I was the most junior officer that was available, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, I know that I may interfere with your concentration when I say this, but please slow down when you give your evidence. In the fall -- and perhaps you can be more specific about the time frame -- were you given any new tasks? Were you dispatched to any location, and who gave you this task?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes. In early October, I can't recall the exact date, I was called by General Vasiljevic and General Tumanov, and the chief of the first department, Colonel Gligorevic was also present so I was called to come to Gligorevic's office and there, I learned that I was to get ready and to depart for Vukovar the next day and to take the post of the counter-intelligence section chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In what unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: In the Guards Motorised Brigade.
