utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I did not have a lot of time to prepare, maybe 20, 30 minutes. They told me that I know what I had to do and that I should authorise my wife to collect my salary if I had not done that before, because otherwise she would not have any means to support herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you told what the objective was for your being sent there at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that since I had experience in counter-intelligence work, that I should improve the operation of the counter-intelligence section in the Motorised Guards Brigade and my perspective would be of use to this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you given any written decision or order for your appointment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No. They told me that the written order would follow and I didn't really need it at all; the oral order sufficed, as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when did you receive this written appointment and who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: When we got back. In fact, during our activities in Vukovar, or rather in Negoslavci at the command, that was the rear command post where the personnel officers were located, I was asked when would I take up the post officially and I said upon my return so this formal appointment to the post of the deputy security chief, I received it once we got back. It was in December 1991. Of course, I was given this written approval by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who, then, signed this written approval?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: The security administration wrote the order but every time a person is transferred, one needs the written approval of the commander of the unit to which one is being posted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: It was Colonel Mile Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but we have to be precise. Mr. Karan, do you remember what happened next? Did you go to Vukovar? When? Where? How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: The next day, around 5.00 or 6.00 a.m., I left the Guards Brigade compound at Topcider by truck and headed towards Vukovar. I arrived there at around 11.00, first to the rear command post in the village of Berak where the assistant to the commander for logistics received me. There were also some other officers there. I told them the reason for my arrival. And soon after that, I was taken in a military vehicle to Negoslavci. That was the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was your final destination? Where did you go to in Negoslavci and who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: My final destination was the house, the premises where the security organ was located in the village of Negoslavci. And I have to say that I waited there several hours to be received, two or three hours. The police officer there would not allow me to get into the offices, first because I didn't have the pass to get into the combat zone, and secondly, I did not have any orders indicating that I was to take up my post. This complicated the matters a little bit, as far as I was concerned, because they wouldn't let me in, but when the chief appeared, I mean Sljivancanin -- in fact I'm not quite clear about the sequence. That's not really important, but perhaps I was allowed to get in a little bit earlier before he arrived, but at any rate, we got introduced to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you introduced yourself to him and he to you, can I then deduce that you did not know him from before?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't know any of the officers in the Guards Brigade before my arrival there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give me the names of the people from the security organ that you met and I can ask you just to be very slow when you give their names and to give me also their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin was the chief of security in the brigade. I met him there. Major Vukasinovic, his first name was Ljubisa, assistant for staff security affairs. Captain Borce Karanfilov, desk officer. And staff sergeant Zoran Momcilovic. He was the clerk. He was the assistant to the desk officer. That's actually -- that was his title. I think that when I got there, I actually did not meet Captain Srecko Borisavljevic. I met him -- later on and I was told also that there were some members of the security organ located in Belgrade, Captain Petar Kovacevic and a warrant officer Grocic. Grocic did not come because he had injured his leg and his leg was in a cast.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in general terms very briefly as an assistant to the chief of security for counter-intelligence work, can you tell us what was your job description? What you were your tasks?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: My task for as the assistant for counter-intelligence work is to cooperate with my colleagues on identifying any signs that would indicate the operation of any intelligence services, sabotage activities, command activities, and other activities that may pose a threat to the unit and its personnel. To be more specific, it was my task to detect any threats to us, the forms of those threats, who actually was behind those threats, and what means are used to actually carry out those activities that posed a threat. At the same time - let me finish, please - we were then supposed to do something about it once we learned all that. And what do we do? How do we counter those activities? What methods and means are we to use? Who should be carrying out those activities within our team, in general, and who has to do each specific stage of each task? So that would be in brief what the counter-intelligence organ or the security organ in the unit does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us move on from the theoretical plain to the practical one. Let us have some practical examples. In your operative work, did you have any instances of any enemy activities within Negoslavci that were of interest to you and that you dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Of course. My colleagues told me about the problems that they faced and their biggest problem was the radio station that was used to guide the enemy fire against our positions and in particular, when some persons -- this would happen when the helicopter would land on the helipad to evacuate the wounded. So we took measures and quite soon we eliminated this threat; in other words, we located the radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any instances of defeatism, any instances of desertion in the unit and was it important for you? Was it something that you analysed and something that you had to respond to as a security organ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Of course low morale, defeatism, and all the other forms of anti-social behaviour were something that was of interest to us because those kind of behaviour affected the combat readiness of the unit and, in the final analysis, the successful execution of the missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will use documents to illustrate specific examples but let us now move on. In your security department, did you have briefings, when these briefings were held, how were they organised in the security organ then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Of course we had such briefings; they were called the daily briefings. But it didn't mean that those briefings had to be held every day. They usually took place in the evenings but sometimes they could take place at other times of day, later or earlier, and sometimes there were days when those briefings were not held at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had been in other units before your posting here as we saw from your CV. When you joined this unit, can you please tell us, did you notice any specific features, any peculiarities in the Guards Brigade that differentiated from the other units, in particular when it comes to the security organ and other parts of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Every former member of the JNA new that Guards Brigade was a special kind of unit and that it had the kind of units that usually belonged to the corps, that usually you would kind in a corps. It had two platoons of the military police. That was not usual. You would not usually find that in a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will not go into the relationship between the military police and the security organ because this had been discussed before, but can you tell me: You, as the security organ, the security section in the Guards Brigade, who were you subordinate to? What organ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: In terms of our work, we were subordinate to the security department of the federal-- cabinet of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have daily correspondence with them? Did you draft reports and send them to them? Who drafted those reports in your section, and what was the purpose of those reports?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: The very purpose of the security service lies in reporting on the security situation in the units within its purview to the superior unit and we did this regularly, every day. There were also some reports, urgent reports, and I was actually in charge of drafting those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how did you actually do that? How did you draft those reports and how did you send them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: At first, it was a bit difficult. I had to write them by hand because my colleagues had not brought the typewriter with them. But as far as I was able to see, these -- our superior command did not mind and only later did we receive the typewriter and then we were able to draft our official documents properly because these were official documents and they had to comply with certain standards, both in formatting and contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with your report? Who actually read those reports?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Of course. Our reports were used when our superior officer in the cabinet of the Federal Secretariat of the National Defence reported to his superior. The security administration used our reports to exercise command and control in the depth of the armies and other units and formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have the first page of Exhibit 819 placed on the -- brought to the screen? Mr. Karan --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to switch on the screen in front of the witness, please. We can see just one portion of it but I think that's what we actually want to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, first of all, do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: It's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please explain, what is this document about?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: This is a daily operations report covering our activities. It's a report we sent on the 12th of October, 1991 to our superiors in the security department of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the last page of the B/C/S for a moment. It's page 10, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Mine. The initials too. It means I wrote it. This is a common procedure with our documents. If this document had been typed up, it would have contained the initials of whoever did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the other reports, the following reports, in terms of substance. Who produced those, if I may put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I myself produced over 9 out of 10 of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who signed them later on?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: This is just a matter of circumstance. I mean the fact that this particular one was not signed by the chief himself. Otherwise, it would have been mandatory for the chief to sign a document being sent on to a superior command. Major Sljivancanin was not physically present and the matter was urgent and the document needed dispatching as soon as possible, which is the reason I signed it, but normally he would sign these.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit 820.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, in very general terms, what is it that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: What we're looking at is a written document from the security department of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence. In duplicate, this is sent in duplicate to the aforementioned office. This is in reference to intelligence about security in units, specifically the units of the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In terms of its substance, we covered this ground during our proofing, does this document reflect what you had submitted to them in a handwritten form?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's an accurate reflection. There may be a word or two was rephrased but the substance remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 3, please. The B/C/S, halfway down the page. While we're waiting for it to show up, Mr. Karan, in your work as an intelligence officer, did you ever come across any situations involving arms dealing? Was this something that you investigated, and who was involved in that sort of activity?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Needless to say, we had such incidents in our area of responsibility. Much to our surprise, these things were done by people who, for professional and other reasons, were not supposed to be doing things like that. We discovered that the Minister of the Interior of the autonomous region was dealing in arms and another two or three of his flunkies from Negoslavci. This was a serious problem not only in an area of combat operations, but also further afield. If you have military equipment and weapons being distributed commercially like that, it can be used to place at risk people who were not affected by the actual fighting. So this was one of our priorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the next page on our screens now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, let me ask you this: Muharem Besic, does that ring a bell? If it does, please tell us something about that person.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I can't see anything on the screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's about to show up.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Muharem Besic, I'm familiar with this person. He had the same rank as I at the time and we had been schoolmates and classmates at the military academy in Belgrade. We established that before my unit arrived in the Vukovar area, they had already left. And he had unlawfully distributed some certificates to persons who weren't authorised security officers. These certificates allowed them to, to all practical intents, become security officers. Of course, once we investigated this, we discovered that there had been such a person in possession of such a certificate, and this person had done things to his own design and not in keeping with the actual rules and regulations. This was important for us so that's why we informed our superior security officer. They informed the administration and the administration did what they were supposed to do in a situation like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This report is based on another one previously produced by yourself. There is reference here to a messenger of the Croatian armed forces being killed by one of those persons in Vukovar; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you produced this report, what status did this person enjoy? Was this person captured, killed? What did your information indicate about the status of this person at the time you found out that the person had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: This person was never a POW. But deep down inside, we knew what had happened. But we just were told at one point that this had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will no longer be requiring this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seems by now to be an undisputed fact that some of the military police units were involved in combat operations. Were you familiar with Mr. Sljivancanin's position on the use of the military police in combat? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes. At our meetings, we had discussions about that, about the fact that military police units were not being used for special purposes in the fighting. So this is what Sljivancanin believed and our team shared his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is not one of the tasks of every security organ to provide technical assessments regarding the use of military police units?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Needless to say, the commander and the assistant commander must advise on the possible use of the military police. They provide technical advice, which is not necessarily accepted by the commander if the commander himself believes that it is necessary to act otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please go into private session for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us what you know about that, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: As operations evolved, the situation in that unit became ever more complex. At one point in time, there was a threat of the situation degenerating into an open refusal to carry out orders, insubordination. There was defeatism, morale was low. This was one of the forms that this unsoldierly behaviour and conduct took on. On the other hand, there was the unsoldierly appearance of soldiers in that unit and such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you react in any way to that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Of course. We submitted reports on the situation daily in that unit and we recommended that this situation be dealt with as soon as possible. As for that particular task, Major Sljivancanin was particularly involved more than anybody else, personally involved, since he had a very good relationship, an excellent relationship, as far as to say, with that particular commander; however other persons were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would wish my learned friend, if he would be kind enough to just directly to the passages in the proofing notes that I've received, because I cannot find anything at all in relation to this topic. We have two proofing notes part one and two, they are both extensive. If you could just show them to me, I would be very grateful. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really glad to have my proofing notes called comprehensive. We did our best, in the case of this particular witness, who never provided any statements to anyone, to practically put together a statement. Just a minute, please. This is a fact that I forgot to mention in my proofing notes and I'll just drop it. I don't think it's that crucial for the OTP to know about this, since we've had a number of written documents about this. But if the Chamber rules that I should not be asking any further questions, I'll just drop this line of questioning. I was going to ask this witness since he's the one who actually produced the documents. Your Honours, the one thing I bore in mind was your guidance to ask the most essential questions. The proofing notes contain over five pages, very comprehensive material, and it may be an omission on my part. If you believe that this is something that I should have stated, in that case, I will just press on with a different line of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Press on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We weren't about to hear anything particularly new anyway. Can you just finish telling us about Mr. Sljivancanin's action in relation to this particular problem, Mr. Karan?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: He took a lot of action, I'd say, in terms of convincing people about things, in terms of seeing people, in terms of advising people. That's as far as his personal involvement was concerned. Needless to say, for our own part, we did some reporting and this became more important, as a consequence. Our superior commands realised that this was a serious situation in that particular unit. I would even go as far as to say, and I know for a fact that the command itself, the brigade command, I mean, was busy with this, was busy trying to overcome this problem. So towards the end of the fighting, the situation sort of died down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. In terms of the security organ, was there a problem concerning the dismissal of reservists from the front line, reservists being sent away before the remaining forces, and is this a problem for a security organ to consider?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: First and foremost, this poses a problem to those planning the actual combat, and, of course, for us too, as a result, since there were several hundreds of reservists who were ours, tried and true, so to speak, these people leave the unit and there's a vacuum that's created and no one to fill it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We looked at the war log. We looked at the entry where Sljivancanin made some adjustments to artillery fire. Do you remember anything specific about this adjustment? You, specifically, the work of the security organ and this in particular.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Of course while I worked at the security administration, I told you that I also covered Bosnia and Herzegovina. We received word at the time that there were acts of sabotage in progress. Shells were being produced in Travnik and in other factories across the country. By the same token, we realised that there was a production line, at the time shells being produced with the specific purpose of being used in Vukovar, in fighting around Vukovar. This was a special signal both for us and for our superiors. This could possibly have been defective ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you another question and then it might be time for our second break. During your daily activities, where were you and where was Mr. Sljivancanin, generally speaking, for as long as you were there? I'm not sure if that makes sense. What was your daily schedule about --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I understand. I understand your question, all right. We agreed at the outset that he, in his capacity as chief, would be at the command, and would, of course, be spending time with us whenever joint activities were being agreed, organised, or specified, whereas the rest of us were at the security organ which was in a separate building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Throughout the month and a half that you were there, even less, perhaps, in the Vukovar theatre of war, did you ever leave Negoslavci, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, that was one of the things agreed initially. When I arrived at the brigade, I faced an uphill struggle simply because I didn't know anyone there. It was only natural and certainly more effective for Major Sljivancanin to do the rounds of the units to try to see for himself, as one should say, what the security situation was, as well as any information relevant for our own assessments, for our analyses and for our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now suggest that we take our break. This session was a little bit unusual but I think it's okay for us to take it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karan, I will now move on to another topic which is of interest to me and I think that you will be able to provide me with some information. Let us move on now to the topic of the relationship between the security organ in the Guards Brigade and other security organs both in the vertical and in the horizontal axes. You told me that your the security organ that was superior to you was in fact the cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence or rather the assistant to the secretary of national defence for security, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, that was so both in technical terms and in terms of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So all the correspondence sent from you to that organ and sent from other organs, the superior organs, and by that I mean primarily the security administration, did it all go through the security organ of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, the SSNO?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: There was no other channel for our documents apart from the security section of the SSNO cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your tour of duty in Vukovar, did you ever have any correspondence that you either sent or received from the security organ of the 1st Military District in Belgrade or from their forward command post in Sid?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, we did not get or send any correspondence to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in Negoslavci performing this task, do you remember whether the officers of the security organ from the 1st Military District visited you? We know that they arrived on the 19th, in the evening of the 19th, but that's another story. But in the period until the fall of Vukovar, until the 18th, do you recall anyone visiting you from there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No. Or in fact sometime in mid-October -- in fact, no, mid-November, the advance unit from the corps arrived. I think that they belonged to the 1st Military District, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that later. Do you know if anyone from the security organ from your section ever went to Sid or Belgrade to receive any instructions or to report to the security organ of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They didn't go or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I'm sure that they didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Operations Group South, were there other security organs apart from the security section of the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you now describe to us the relationship between your security section and the security organs in the other units that were part of the Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. The security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade was the security organ just for the Guards Motorised Brigade. All the other units that were part of the OG South had their own security organs. There was no chain of command from the chief of security in the Guards Brigade leading down to the security organs in those other units. In other words, the chief of security in the Guards Motorised Brigade was not the superior officer for any security organ that was part of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order for your section and for your chief to become superior to the other security organs, who can decide that? Who can make decisions changing the structure and the chain of command in technical terms in the security organ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: For the security organ in the Guards Motorised Brigade to become the superior security organ for the entire Operations Group South, it would first have to change its name from section to department and only the Federal Secretary of National Defence or a person authorised by him, that would be the chief of the security administration, could make such a decision. That would have to be done in writing defining the structure of the new security organ, its tasks, and the channels through which reports would be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your correspondence with the security department in the SSNO, and the security administration through this department, did anyone ever address your organ as the security organ of the OG South?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, never, because we were never such an organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the reports and documents that you yourself sent to those institutions, did you at any point state that you represented the security organ of the OG South?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if at some point during your tour of duty, whether the 80th Motorised Brigade became part of the OG South, I mean the 80th Motorised Brigade from Kragujevac and did you have any contact with its security organ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think that some 10 days before the 80th Kragujevac Brigade was to be deployed in Vukovar, we, at the section, were visited by two representatives of their superior command, two security officers from their superior command or rather that was the Kragujevac corps, I remember clearly that this was Lieutenant-Colonel Zika Petrovic who had worked with me in Bijeljina. He was the security officer there before I got there. We then informed them of the situation in the field. In other words, we presented to them the overall counter-intelligence situation that their unit would face once it was deployed in the combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Vukosavljevic Dragi mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, I met him a few days after their unit was deployed in the combat zone. He actually reported to us. In fact, he came to see us in the security section.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of his visit, if you remember, and what happened then? Was there any conversation? Can you describe the situation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Well, he had come to the combat zone and quite naturally, security officers should visit their opposite numbers in the other unit and we did not present the situation for his unit in the field because he had already been briefed by his superior command or, rather, by the security organ of the Kragujevac Corps. So we had a brief exchange and we agreed that if there were any problems, we would meet or talk, get in touch. Something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Negoslavci, did Dragi Vukosavljevic or, indeed, any other security officer from the 80th Brigade or any other unit give you any written or oral reports?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, there were no oral or written reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he or any other officer from that unit or similar units ever get from you any task whatsoever? I mean technical instructions from the security organ, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, we could not issue any tasks to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he or any other security officer or organ from any other unit that was part of OG South at any point attend any briefings of your section?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship between your security section and the security administration? What was the chain of command there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Do you mean in terms of reporting? In terms of reporting, we first reported to the security department of the cabinet of the Federal Secretariat of the National Defence and then they reported to the security administration. According to our rules and regulations, we were not supposed to send any reports or indeed to address the security administration directly at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now touch upon a different topic briefly. Mr. Karan, in the period while you were there, did you know if there were any civilian authorities in Negoslavci and, if yes, which authorities were there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout this period, we're talking about the period from my arrival until the end of fighting or, rather, our pull-out back to Belgrade, the local police station was operational and it had all the necessary aspects of a police station. They had their police commander, the duty roster, vehicle, communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know which authority actually controlled its work, under whose jurisdiction was it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: They were under the jurisdiction of the Minister of the Interior, and I guess that's who they reported to, but I didn't really get involved in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that Boro Bogunovic, the Minister of the Interior that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, what was the relationship between the military authorities that you were part of, the military structure, and the police station? Was it a relationship in which there was subordination? Was that the nature of your relationship?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, there was no subordination. They could not -- there could not be subordination. They were the police and they carried out their own tasks within their own purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the police commander in this station?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: There were two of them, one of them got killed. I can't recall his name, but I do know that the other person's name was Kovacevic. Ilija Kovacevic, that was his full name. He was a professional police officer. He had graduated from the police school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard evidence here about the regime governing the movement of all people in the zone of combat and in Negoslavci. Do you know whether this police station was subjected to the same regime? Was there any coordination here or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Let me be specific. The roots should, in a way, be under the jurisdiction of the local police, but the situation in the combat zone in Vukovar was such that they had to agree to a different regime because it suited them in light of their -- the equipment that they had, for -- to let our military police perform those tasks. I think that was a little infringement of the actual jurisdiction of the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you able to cooperate well with them? Were you able to communicate well with them, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Well, we knew them and we changed information and so on, but we didn't really interfere with their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karan, what did you know about the Vukovar Hospital during the actual fighting prior to the 18th of November? You, as a security officer, did you have any information that you believed to be important?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Of course. We had our own information that we retrieved in our capacity as security officers. However, we also received guidance and documents containing guidance from our superiors and from the security organ of the cabinet of the federal secretary, things about the hospital and about what happened in and around the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the gist of these reports?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: To put it in the simplest possible terms, the gist was that the hospital was not only a hospital. Rather, reports suggested that it was occasionally used as a place or a position from which fire was opened on our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit 824 brought up on our screens for the witness's benefit. Briefly, this is a covering letter. Let's not dwell any more time than necessary on this. Can we please go to page 2 of this exhibit. Halfway down the page, and the upper half as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, can you please comment on the second paragraph, the one we are looking at? Does that bring to mind specific information of what we are talking about now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: What I'm looking at is a document containing guidance or instructions from the security organ to -- of the security administration to the security organ of the Guards Brigade through the security section or department of the cabinet of the Federal Minister for National Defence. On the face of this document, you can see that they are informing us about one of the defence centres of the MUP forces as being inside the Vukovar Hospital and as holding certain ZNG members, while other members of the MUP were still at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you received something like this, what does it tell you? How do you use it for your intelligence work?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, this at any report is first of all brought to the attention of your command and then all the units along that particular axis down the chain of command. What do we use it for? We use it as a foundation for any further assessments, for any of our counter-intelligence assessments regarding the situation prevailing in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, the 18th of November, 1991, what does that tell you? What is the first thing that springs to mind?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: The first thing that springs to mind is Vukovar actually fell that day, which means our units took the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you briefly: Is there any personal recollection that you associate with that date, something you did on that date? We talked and we didn't find out much, but do you remember yourself doing anything in particular on that day?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: The 18th, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me try to be a little more specific. Did you do anything about the surrender of the Mitnica Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, I was in no way involved in that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on to the following day. During your actual proofing, I was not able to obtain from you anything that was helpful at all in terms of this testimony. It was different with the 18th. But can you tell us whether on the 19th, you went to the Vukovar Hospital? When? Can you tell us what you remember about that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I did go there, yes. I went to the Vukovar Hospital because I was told by Major Sljivancanin to go there. I think I arrived sometime after lunchtime, at about 2.00 or 3.00 p.m. It has been 15 years, after all, and I haven't exactly been rehashing this since the events at the time and it's very difficult to be very specific about the time line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you got to the hospital, who did you find there? Who did you see, describe the scene? How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I got there from Negoslavci. I took the road to Vukovar. A driver who knew the way took me there. When I came there, I found men from our own unit. More specifically, members of the police. Inside, I met Captain Simic and I knew that he was the commander of the unit that was in and around the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there an exchange between the two of you? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: It was a brief exchange between us and one thing that struck me as noteworthy is he pointed out a passerby and said: This is Dr. Njavro, just for you to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did that strike you as noteworthy, him mentioning that name or that person? Why do you think he did that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Because over the previous days and weeks, we had been talking about the Vukovar Hospital doctors and about the way the hospital was organised, who was in charge, who were the doctors, that sort of thing. And Njavro was a familiar name had that had cropped up many times before but I didn't know what this man actually looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I parted ways with Simic soon after. I stopped Dr. Njavro to inquire about a schoolmate of mine who was also working as a doctor at the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you share his name with us? I mean your schoolmate that you asked Njavro about?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Radomir Dejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat that name for us?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Radomir Dejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you want to know about that person in particular?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: We were schoolmates for four years in high school. I know he was a resident of Bobota. I had been at his wedding and I knew that he was now an employee of the Vukovar Hospital. I was curious to know what had become of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did Njavro tell you, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: He said he had left for Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin called me and asked me to go to a specific room in the hospital grounds, it's a small room right next to the hospital entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you see there, tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I saw Dr. Bosanac, Vesna Bosanac, who was a familiar name and face. I had seen her face on TV previously so I recognised her immediately. Mr. Sljivancanin told me that I should stay with them in that room, since there were a number of other people there, and to watch them, to put it in the simplest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I approached this driver who was also a military police officer. I told him to stand at the door, to watch the door so that nobody would disturb us inside. The atmosphere was such that it was impossible to avoid such a conversation, so Dr. Bosanac started introducing all these people to me which was the first time I ever set eyes on this person that she said was Marin Vidic, Bili. I had imagined him quite differently. His hair was unkempt, he was unshaven, he was thin as a rake and blond. The other person he named was Anton Avric who was a paramedic who had arrived from Zagreb to help out. She introduced Njavro, she hadn't realised that I had met him before. We stayed in that room for about an hour. It's difficult to be specific. I know, because at one point, I allowed Dr. Bosanac to use the phone, but only over the interphone so that I, too, was able to monitor the conversation. There is one thing that I'm forgetting. That sticks with me. I became angry immediately, even before the whole thing began. There was a foreigner there, a tall man, long, blond hair from the Red Cross with a white coat. I learned later that this was the ICRC representative there, Borsinger. Another thing that struck me at the time. In my presence, Dr. Bosanac gave the ICRC man some documents. I became quite angry and informed Sljivancanin immediately that she had provided this man with a list of some kind. We didn't know what this list was about. It looked like a list of names. And then Sljivancanin said: Here, I have one too that I got from her. She told me this was the same list as the one she'd handed to the ICRC man previously. She said that the two lists were consistent. Needless to say, I was none too happy about this. I said I didn't think it was a good thing that we didn't know what she had actually given him but as far as I remember, Sljivancanin said well that's all right. I just leave it like that. We're not taking it away from them now. I assume that he believed that the list given to the ICRC man was the same list that she had given to us. I had a look and I realised that it was nothing at all like the list that had been given to the ICRC man. It struck me more as a more minor list containing names of persons. Names were crossed out on it, names were added to it, and copied. It seemed like somebody was playing a random game using a telephone directory. That's what it looked like. It was of little, if any, use to us. Sljivancanin left and I stayed with them. We started talking. In the meantime, Dr. Bosanac had picked up the phone twice. Calls from Vinkovci, I assume, from the Vinkovci operations zone. I think there was a call from Zagreb, too. It was Hebrang's secretary. While I was with them in that room, Dr. Bosanac surprised me by doing something in particular, something that under the circumstances was not appropriate. She asked me about my name. I said, "Mladen." "Where are you from," she said. "Petrova Gora," I replied. She thought that I was from the Petrova Gora in Vukovar, I assume. Since she believed me to be a Croat from Vukovar, she said: "Help. Help us," without explaining what exactly what she meant. During those conversations, I interrupted her conversation with Zagreb, the secretary wanted to know who was on the line and I was angry about her inquiring. She even order offered to me a rank in the Croatian army, major general, the rank of major general, as some sort of a bribe, this secretary, which really riled me. She didn't really provide any details of what I would be expected to do or how I was expected to help. She just said, "Help us." On the other hand -- there were four of them, right. They often looked up to the ceiling, there were some books or documents apparently on top of a shelf. There was a huge black bag which looked a bit like a bin liner to me. It was quite big and quite black. I looked in the same direction and my take was there was something there that was concealed. The first thought that struck me, it might be something that was likely to put me at risk. I said: "What is it?" They failed to answer. At my own risk, I climbed a chair and pulled the bag down. I opened the bag and realised that there was a large number of bank notes inside, money. I immediately informed Major Sljivancanin about this. He replied: "What shall we do about that?" And I said, based on my previous experience, as soon -- as it's money, the best thing is to be rid of it as soon as possible because people start talking in no time at all. I suggested for this money to be handed over to some sort of a commission to be counted. I suggested that a report be drafted and that we wait for further instructions from our superior security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you continue, did you ask Bosanac and the other people where that money was from?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I asked her who this money belonged to and she said that this was the money from the -- of the Crisis Staff, and I immediately got this idea that I should really check whether the Serb doctors had received their salaries too, because she said that these were -- this was the money for the salaries of the Crisis Staff. And then I went to the room where the Serb medical staff from the hospital was, where they gathered, and I asked female doctor whether they had been receiving salaries in the previous period and she said, "No, we haven't." Then I complied with -- after Major Sljivancanin said that he agreed with my suggestion, telling me to immediately go to Negoslavci to set-up the commission that would count the money and then report to the superior security organ and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, this room where the Serb medical staff was, where was that room in relation to the room where you were with Dr. Bosanac and the others?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: You had a line of vision from one room to the other. Let me explain this. This was a quadrangular hallway and, if you walked into the hospital, the room where with Dr. Bosanac was to the right and this other room was a small room to the left on the ground floor in the lobby, in fact, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from these two rooms that you said you visited, did you go to any other places in the Vukovar Hospital on that date?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when did you leave the hospital, not the exact time, but whether it was after nightfall, dusk, daytime?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: It was in the late afternoon. I think dusk, 5.00, 4.00, 6.00 p.m., I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. We're not asking you to. During that evening and night, did you go to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the name -- Dr. Stanojevic and Dr. Ivankovic, do these names mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, these are the doctors that worked in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: They were Serb doctors. They were ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the name Bogdan Kuzmic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nikola Dukic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay in the hospital on that day when you got in and got out and in the area where you actually were, were you able to see any other members of the Serb forces, the Territorial Defence, the volunteers, apart from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No. Apart from Major Simic's unit, I didn't see anyone else. In fact, I assumed that the personnel there were members of his unit and there were no other units there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you upon your return to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: I set up this commission. He we did what we were tasked to do. We drafted the report for the security organ of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary of National Defence and we waited for the chief to come in order to report to him on our daily activities. This was the regular briefing that we did almost every day, because he needed to be briefed on what the other security organs had been doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So did you see Sljivancanin that evening?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive your tasks for the next day then, if you can recall what were you talking about and who was given which task?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that our task for the next day -- I mean our counter-intelligence activities was related to the evacuation of the wounded and the sick from the hospital. Now, if your question was what my task was, then I can tell you that Sljivancanin told me that the two of us would go to the hospital in the morning and that persons or rather security officers from the security administration would go with us to assist us. In other words, he informed me that some people from the security administration would come and that a group of doctors from Novi Sad would also take part in this task, seven or eight doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you at that time what tasks would have to be done in the hospital, what lay ahead for you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: When he issued the tasks, he told me that I would be there to make sure that the doctors would be able to perform a selection of the wounded and so on. We knew - we had received information that in the previous days, and in fact even after the 18th, after the surrender of the Mitnica Battalion - those who did not want to surrender had withdrawn to the hospital and that they were dressing up as medical staff or that they were pretending that they were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You, as a security officer, as a counter-intelligence operative, you have this kind of information. What does this information mean to you in terms of organising the evacuation of the wounded and the sick, and the circumstances in which this evacuation would take place?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: This means that there is a high level of risk because we did not know anything about the intentions of those people, why they had come to the hospital, and we had previous intelligence that they were armed and we knew that these were the most extreme elements because they had refused to surrender. This was a high-risk situation that required us to address this task in a very serious manner and I think that the very presence of the doctors, the presence of the security officers from the superior command really showed how important this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that meeting with Mr. Sljivancanin, was there any discussion as to what would be done with the persons who were hiding among the medical staff or the wounded?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, Ljubisa Vukasinovic. The task was to transfer those persons to the barracks and then from the barracks to transfer them immediately to Sremska Mitrovica. And I have to note here that I did not perform the triage. This was not my task. It was my task to make sure that the doctors doing the job would do that in such a way, in a safe environment, in other words, that nothing would happen to those doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what tasks were issued to your other colleagues for the next day? Did they have any tasks pertaining to this evacuation or what?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Captain Karanfilov was supposed to go to the shelter that had been used by the commander of the defence of Vukovar and to gather the documents there and to inventory the things that could be found there in those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, at that time, did you hear about the Zagreb Agreement, as we call it? Did you hear that there had been negotiations going on about the evacuation of the wounded and the sick from the hospital between the ministry -- the health ministry in Zagreb and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In those days, were you told that negotiations had been going on in Negoslavci between some JNA officers on the one side and the ICRC and the ECMM regarding this very same issue?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No. I did not really analyse any events that were in the public domain, so to speak. I don't know much about that, because I had other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, perhaps, see Vesna Bosanac that evening? Do you know what happened to her?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No. When I left the hospital, I didn't see her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone else had talked to her?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes, I know that Major Sljivancanin talked to her because he told us that later, sometime after the briefing that we had, that was the very short briefing. I assumed that from there, went to the command -- he didn't tell us where he was going, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you did not see her?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else who was brought to the building where your section was?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Yes. Marin Vidic, Bili, was brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now hear from you about this event. When was that? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Well, I can't really remember because of the time that has elapsed, at what time it happened. I am sure that this was before midnight, maybe an hour or two hours before midnight. I know that because I know at what time we had briefing. It was maybe an hour or two hours after the briefing. He was brought there to the offices of the security organ in Negoslavci. And since I knew him from before, I had already talked to him. He was offered a seat. And he is the kind of man that adapts fairly quickly to a new environment. And he was able to create a relaxed atmosphere if you compare it to the atmosphere would be able to create, especially in circumstances where that person would be arrested. He asked for something to drink, some refreshments, and it was interesting for me to note that he had his guitar with him. We allowed him to keep it. We didn't really mind. And the fact that had he brought his guitar with him and the fact that he was so relaxed in his communication with us -- we knew that he was the government commissioner, but what really surprised me was that spoke against his erstwhile fellow thinkers in political terms. He criticised the official policy of his government. He spoke against Tudjman, and I felt that this could be put to some use in propaganda terms, and I immediately called the forensic technicians asking hem them to record that and he agreed to being recorded. I thought that if such a tape could be provided to the Belgrade TV in Serbia, that some effects could be achieved, some positive effects. So, as all this equipment was being set up, I asked him: If you can play the guitar, I'm sure you can sing too. And I have no doubt that he's a top-notch singer in his own right, I can say that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was with you there throughout this time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: Captain Karanfilov, in and out of the room, but he was with us most of the time. I was there, the forensic technician who was supposed to do the recording, I think his name was Cekic, and later on, Major Sljivancanin joined us soon after Marin Vidic had been brought in. We had hardly started this little activity that I had come up with. Sljivancanin talked to him briefly between the songs that he sang for us. In the meantime, as all of this was going on, General Tumanov and General Vasiljevic arrived. I hadn't realised that they were actually in the combat zone or there. One thing that was striking is that one of them refused to exchange greetings with him. We stayed there for a while talking. It was more about the political situation in Croatia and the decision of the Croatian authorities to declare the JNA an occupation army. We tried to explain that there was no way we could be an occupation army in our own country, that we were not the enemy of the Croatian people. Needless to say, he agreed with us at this time. That's where our conversation was headed. We knew that he was a political figure, someone appointed by the Zagreb-based government, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he at one point taken away from there or did he stay with you throughout?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No. We dropped this idea of mine. I think Vasiljevic was the one who didn't want that or someone. Anyway, the idea was dropped. They said there was no need to do anything like that where it might even be a damaging thing for our public image, somebody said. So we decided to do something more earnest, more serious. We decided for him to give a statement to the police which would carry some weight later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to explain something. The forensic technicians, that particular department, which unit did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another one and a half questions and we'll be wrapping up for the day. Mr. Karan, where was Mr. Sljivancanin sleeping throughout his time in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: We were all in the same room, crowded, all of the security officers. This was a room adjacent to the room in which we worked. We worked out that this was the most practical thing for us to do and we were all there with the exception of his driver, who was in a different room in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That evening, once Sljivancanin had arrived, which you say occurred soon after Marin Vidic had been brought in, did he leave the building again that evening, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN
utterances.text: No, he didn't. We all slept there and the next morning, we all woke up. Actually, I was the one who woke everybody else, since I am an early riser myself, and we were off to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is a perfect moment for us to call it a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We adjourn now to resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 29th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
